newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Treasurer Peters says confident in economy.
newsitem.headline: NZ Treasurer Peters says confident in economy.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters on Friday welcomed recent falls in interest rates and said he expected a restoration of business confidence.

In an interview with Reuters in his home electorate of Tauranga, Peters said recent surveys showing a decline in business confidence had been carried out when significant information was not fully known.
"I think it is all relative. I think there will be a restoration of confidence. It is clear the economy has troughed some time ago and things are beginning to pick up."
Recent data has painted a picture of a sluggish New Zealand economy but one in which growth may be starting to bottom out, helped by lower interest rates and a slightly softer dollar.
Peters added his voice to that of Finance Minister Bill Birch who said on Friday that New Zealand deserved a triple A credit rating from major rating agencies rather than its AA+.
"We are deserving of one. When the two (rating) institutions Standard and Poor's and Moody's come visiting, which is pretty soon, we have got some good news to tell them," he said.

"I expect their assessment to reflect the reality of an economy which is being soundly managed with healthy surpluses, a slightly slower debt repayment schedule, and nevertheless with areas of critical social expenditure that can't be ignored being addressed."

Another factor was the removal of "the instability factor of politics", he said, referring to the formation of the coalition government between his nationalist New Zealand First party and the centre-right National Party in December.
Peters said the date of the 1997/98 budget had not yet been fixed but would be delivered in mid to late June.
Asked how he thought financial markets would react to the budget, he said: "I think they will react positively because we are getting the message over.

"The days of dramatic budget surprises are over. The March 4 budget policy statement clearly set out where we intend to go, now it is a matter of the detail. There will be some good news for a lot of people."
Peters said a planned September referendum on compulsory superannuation was not causing uncertainties for long-term budget forecasting, as some economic commentators fear.
The referendum may herald the introduction of a new government-regulated but privately managed pension savings scheme which has been dubbed "compulsory super".

Peters reiterated that he believed the speed of the New Zealand dollar's rise had been arrested. The strength of the dollar has started to be cited by some export companies as pressure on their business performance and competitive edge.
"That dollar rose 26 percent in the three years to December (1996). If anyone is concerned about exporters they will (welcome) that the velocity of it has been arrested," he said.
